title: Algebra, Trigonometry & Precalculus Toolkit
subject: Algebra & Precalc
summary: A fast, targeted rebuild of the algebra, function, trig and estimation skills that calculus and physics assume, aimed at a chemist who has the ideas but has lost the reflexes. Ends with the dimensional-analysis and small-quantity approximation habits physicists use daily.

units.title: Algebraic Fluency
units.summary: Rebuild the manipulation reflexes physics assumes: exponent and radical rules, factoring, completing the square, linear systems, inequalities and absolute values; chemists use these daily in equilibrium and kinetics algebra.

lessons.title: Symbolic manipulation: exponents, radicals, and rational expressions
objectives: Simplify expressions using the exponent laws (product, quotient, power, negative and zero exponents) without a calculator, including fractional exponents such as x^(3/2).
Convert fluently between radical form and rational-exponent form and rationalise a denominator.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide rational expressions by finding a common denominator and cancelling only common factors.
Rearrange a formula to isolate a chosen variable (e.g. solve PV = nRT for T, or K = [C][D]/([A][B]) for [D]) and state each algebraic step's justification.
Identify and avoid the standard algebra errors: (a+b)^2 = a^2+b^2, cancelling terms instead of factors, and dropping the square-root sign ambiguity.

lessons.title: Factoring, completing the square, and the quadratic formula
objectives: Factor polynomials using greatest common factor, difference of squares/cubes, and trinomial methods.
Complete the square for ax^2+bx+c and read off the vertex and the axis of symmetry.
Derive the quadratic formula by completing the square and use the discriminant to predict the number and type of roots.
Solve a quadratic equilibrium expression (e.g. x^2/(c-x) = K for a weak acid) and decide which root is physically admissible.
Solve equations that are quadratic in disguise by substitution (e.g. x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0).

lessons.title: Linear equations, systems, inequalities, and absolute values
objectives: Solve systems of two and three linear equations by substitution and elimination and recognise inconsistent and dependent systems.
Solve linear and compound inequalities, expressing the answer as an interval, and explain when the inequality sign flips.
Solve equations and inequalities involving |x - a| by splitting into cases or using the distance interpretation.
Set up and solve a mixing, stoichiometry or dilution word problem as a linear system (e.g. two solutions combined to a target concentration).
Solve a quadratic or rational inequality by sign analysis on intervals.

units.title: Functions and Graphs
units.summary: Function notation, domain and range, composition, inverses, transformations of graphs, polynomials and rational functions; the vocabulary every later calculus and physics derivation is written in.

lessons.title: Functions: notation, domain and range, composition, and inverses
objectives: Evaluate a function given by formula, table or graph, and use the vertical line test to decide whether a relation is a function.
Determine the domain and range of a function built from polynomials, radicals, quotients and logarithms.
Form f(g(x)) and g(f(x)), determine the domain of a composite, and decompose a composite into inner and outer functions (the skill behind the chain rule).
Decide whether a function is one-to-one, find its inverse algebraically, and sketch the inverse as a reflection across y = x.
Distinguish a function from its value, and write a physical relation (e.g. P(V) at fixed T) as a function with stated domain.

lessons.title: Graph transformations, symmetry, and average rate of change
objectives: Sketch y = a f(b(x - h)) + k from the graph of f by applying shifts, stretches and reflections in the correct order.
Classify a function as even, odd, or neither algebraically and from its graph, and state what that implies for the integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval (to be proved later).
Compute the average rate of change (slope of a secant line) of a function over an interval and interpret its units.
Identify intervals of increase/decrease and local extrema from a graph and relate them to the sign of the rate of change.
Write a piecewise function (e.g. the potential of a step barrier) and graph it, marking open and closed endpoints.

lessons.title: Polynomials and rational functions: division, zeros, asymptotes, partial fractions
objectives: Divide polynomials using long division and synthetic division and state the remainder theorem and factor theorem.
Find all rational zeros of a polynomial with the rational zeros theorem, and use multiplicity to describe end behaviour and the graph at each zero.
Find vertical, horizontal and oblique asymptotes and holes of a rational function and sketch its graph.
Decompose a proper rational function into partial fractions (distinct linear, repeated linear, and irreducible quadratic factors), the algebra used later in integration and Laplace transforms.
Explain why the fundamental theorem of algebra implies that an nth-degree polynomial has n complex roots counted with multiplicity.

units.title: Exponentials and Logarithms
units.summary: Exponential and logarithmic functions, their laws, and modelling with them; the language of Arrhenius kinetics, Beer-Lambert absorbance, pH, half-lives and Boltzmann factors.

lessons.title: Exponential and logarithmic functions and their laws
objectives: Graph y = b^x and y = log_b x, state their domains and ranges, and explain why they are inverses.
Apply the three log laws (product, quotient, power) and the change-of-base formula to expand, combine, and evaluate logarithms by hand.
Solve exponential and logarithmic equations, and check for extraneous solutions.
Define e as the base for which d/dx of b^x equals b^x (previewing calculus) and convert any base to base e via b^x = e^(x ln b).
Use logs for chemistry: compute pH from [H+], and solve the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT) for Ea given two rate constants at two temperatures.

lessons.title: Exponential models: growth, decay, and semi-log plots
objectives: Model growth or decay as N(t) = N0 e^(kt) and convert between the rate constant k, the half-life, and the doubling time.
Use semi-log and log-log plots to turn exponentials and power laws into straight lines and extract the parameters from the slope and intercept.
Linearise first-order kinetics data (ln[A] versus t) and an Arrhenius data set (ln k versus 1/T) and extract k and Ea from a fit.
Apply Beer-Lambert A = epsilon l c and radioactive decay as the same exponential-decay mathematics.
Solve compound-interest and continuous-compounding problems and recognise that (1 + 1/n)^n tends to e.

units.title: Trigonometry
units.summary: Angles and radians, the unit circle, the six trig functions and their inverses, graphs of sinusoids, identities, and solving triangles: the geometry behind waves, orbitals, and rotations.

lessons.title: Angles, radians, and the unit circle
objectives: Convert between degrees and radians and compute arc length s = r theta and sector area A = r^2 theta / 2.
State from memory the sine and cosine of 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees (and equivalents in radians) and extend them to all four quadrants using reference angles.
Define cos theta and sin theta as the coordinates of a point on the unit circle and derive the identity sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.
Compute angular velocity omega = theta / t and relate it to linear speed v = r omega.
Identify the quadrant of an angle and the sign of each trig function there.

readings.title: Unit Circle: Sine and Cosine Functions

lessons.title: Right-triangle trigonometry, the other four functions, and inverse trig
objectives: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find unknown sides and angles of a right triangle and resolve a vector into components.
Define tan, cot, sec, csc from sin and cos and state their domains and signs by quadrant.
Define arcsin, arccos, arctan, state their principal-value ranges, and evaluate expressions such as sin(arccos x) by drawing a triangle.
Explain why a restricted domain is needed for an inverse trig function, using the horizontal line test.

lessons.title: Graphs of sinusoids: amplitude, period, phase, and oscillation models
objectives: Read amplitude, period, angular frequency, phase shift and midline from y = A sin(Bx - C) + D and sketch it.
Write a sinusoid from a graph or from a verbal description (e.g. a mass on a spring at t = 0 at maximum displacement).
Graph tan, cot, sec, csc, identifying the vertical asymptotes and period of each.
Relate frequency f, angular frequency omega, and period T by omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi / T and give the units of each.
Model simple harmonic motion x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi) and explain the physical meaning of phi.

lessons.title: Trigonometric identities
objectives: Prove the Pythagorean, reciprocal and quotient identities and derive 1 + tan^2 = sec^2 from sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.
Use the sum and difference formulas for sine and cosine, and derive the double-angle and half-angle formulas from them.
Rewrite sin^2 and cos^2 in terms of cos 2theta (the power-reduction formulas), the move that makes integrals like the integral of sin^2 doable.
Convert products to sums and sums to products, e.g. to see beats between two close frequencies.
Verify an identity by transforming one side only, without assuming the result.

lessons.title: Solving trig equations, general triangles, and the small-angle approximation
objectives: Solve trigonometric equations, finding all solutions in an interval and the general solution with +2 pi n.
Use the law of sines and law of cosines to solve a non-right triangle, and the ambiguous case of SSA.
Compute the area of a triangle as (1/2) a b sin C.
State and justify, numerically, the small-angle approximations sin theta ~ theta, tan theta ~ theta, cos theta ~ 1 - theta^2/2, and give the error at 5 and 20 degrees.
Apply the small-angle approximation to the pendulum to turn the nonlinear equation into simple harmonic motion.

units.title: Complex Numbers, Vectors, and Coordinates
units.summary: Complex arithmetic and polar form (the gateway to Euler's formula and wavefunctions), vectors, and polar and parametric coordinates.

lessons.title: Complex numbers: arithmetic, polar form, and Euler's formula
objectives: Add, multiply, divide and conjugate complex numbers z = a + bi and compute |z|, arg z, and Re and Im parts.
Convert between rectangular and polar form z = r e^(i theta) and multiply and divide in polar form by multiplying moduli and adding angles.
State Euler's formula e^(i theta) = cos theta + i sin theta, and use it to re-derive the sum formulas for sine and cosine.
Find all n roots of z^n = w using De Moivre's theorem and place them on the complex plane.
Explain why a complex quadratic has conjugate roots when the coefficients are real and how this relates to oscillating solutions (chemistry: the phase factors in wavefunctions like e^(ikx)).

lessons.title: Vectors, polar coordinates, and parametric curves
objectives: Represent a vector in components and in magnitude-direction form and add, subtract and scale vectors geometrically and algebraically.
Compute dot products and use them to find the angle between two vectors and the component of one along another.
Convert between polar (r, theta) and rectangular (x, y) coordinates and sketch simple polar curves (circle, cardioid, rose).
Describe a curve parametrically (x(t), y(t)) and eliminate the parameter, e.g. for projectile motion and circular motion.
Write the equation of a conic in rectangular form and recognise ellipse, parabola and hyperbola from the equation (orbits, preview).

units.title: Estimation, Dimensions, and Approximation
units.summary: Dimensional analysis, order-of-magnitude estimation, sequences and the binomial theorem, and small-quantity approximations: the habits that let physicists check and simplify a result before computing it.

lessons.title: Dimensional analysis and order-of-magnitude estimation
objectives: Express a physical quantity's dimensions in M, L, T (and temperature, charge) and check that every equation is dimensionally consistent.
Use dimensional analysis to derive the scaling of a result, e.g. the period of a pendulum T ~ sqrt(l/g), or the radius of a blast wave from energy and density, up to a dimensionless constant.
Convert units reliably, including between SI and cgs and between J/mol, eV and kcal/mol.
Make a Fermi estimate (e.g. number of molecules in a breath, or atoms in a grain of salt) by decomposing it into factors, stating uncertainty in orders of magnitude.
Use a dimensionless group (such as E/kT, the Boltzmann factor argument) to decide which regime a problem is in.

lessons.title: Sequences, the binomial theorem, and approximation of small quantities
objectives: Sum an arithmetic and a geometric series and evaluate sigma notation, including the infinite geometric series with |r| < 1.
Expand (a + b)^n with the binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle, and compute binomial coefficients nCk.
Use the binomial approximation (1 + x)^p ~ 1 + p x for |x| << 1 to simplify expressions such as 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) and gravitational potential corrections.
Estimate the error of a first- or second-order approximation by comparing against the exact value on a calculator.
Count arrangements and combinations with factorials (preview of statistical mechanics counting of microstates).
